title: Chapter 6: Dry by Midnight
blurb: Ravi has until midnight to keep a promise to a mould, and when it is kept the lift grows a new button.

blocks.text: Imogen read the Felt's complaint off the notice board aloud, in the voice you'd use to read a sick note back to the child who'd forged it: low, kind, careful with every word.

"'Trespass. The caretaker entered by the panel without leave. The Felt, head tenant, floor five.'" The grey letters had spread again since the small hours. The full stop had gone furry. "Ruling at midnight. So by midnight, Ravi, you'll owe a mould an apology or an order." She let that sit. "Two paths here."
I had never apologised to a mould in my life. I found I already knew which path I was on.
"Do you mind?" she said, and took a laser measure out of her coat pocket, smaller than Aled's, and didn't wait to find out.

She gave floor 5 ten minutes by her watch. She walked the corridor with the red dot running ahead of her on the brown lino, wrote in a little black notebook, and never once looked surprised. She measured the corridor end to end and underlined the number.
I followed with my hands in my pockets. They'd been swollen for two and a half days, hot and tight across the knuckles, and in pockets nobody had to look at them.

I talked about the floor. I couldn't seem to stop. "There's a dip here, feel that? Somebody's notched a joist for a pipe run and never plated it. It's not going anywhere, it's just tired. And the lino's lifting there, that's damp coming up, that's on the list—"
"Ravi."
"—and what are the joists even bearing on, because this corridor's longer than the building—"
"Ravi." Lower. "I'm not Aled. I'm not writing up your floor."
She stopped at the riser panel near the unnumbered door and looked at it with her pen against her lip. The mushroom smell was strong there. She didn't touch it.
"Is this where?"
"That's where."
"Hm," she said, and wrote one short word, and walked back to the lift.
She pressed G herself on the way down, without looking, as if she'd been pressing that panel all her life.
Dusty lifted his head from his mat and looked at Imogen the way he looks at post that's all brown envelopes, then put his chin back on his paws and sighed.
"Hello, you," she said to him, warmly. He didn't do anything at all.
Kit's parcel was still on the tiles by the service-lift doors. Neither of us looked at it.
She took an envelope out of her bag. Cream, heavy, the Greyfold name pressed into the flap.

"Option one," she said. "You give the Trust your notice, you leave Wickline Street quietly, and Greyfold writes you a reference. Signed by a partner. For someone with your history, that opens doors that have been shut for four years." She held it out. "Option two is midnight. And the midnight after that."
I took it, because it would have been odd not to. Getting it open took a while. She didn't offer to help, which I was grateful for.

It was a good reference. It said I had an unusual eye for structural defects, which was a funny thing for Greyfold to say. Underneath, above a dotted line with my name typed below it, a third paragraph said that in consideration of the reference I would disclose to no person the condition, layout or history of any property in which Greyfold Property Partners held an interest, without the firm's written consent.
I read it twice. The second time my lips moved, the way they do, and Imogen waited with her hands folded, as if she'd known they would.
"Those joists on five," I said. "If they're timber, they're bearing on something I haven't found. I'd want a look at the ends before I said anything about that floor to anyone."
"Ravi."
"No," I said. "Thank you. It's got a confidentiality clause in it."
"They all do. It's standard."
"Then it'll be standard for whoever signs it." I folded the letter back along its creases, which took longer than it should have, and held it out.
She looked at my hands, then my face, and her voice came down another notch. "Keep it. Think about it."
"I've thought about it."
She took it back and checked her watch. "Then I'm late, and I'm never late." At the front door she looked up at the top hinge, where the door rubs. "Midnight, Ravi," she said. "Be nice to it."
The door scraped the frame on her way out. Aled had the van running.
I'd known what 5-1's door wanted since the night I took it. What I hadn't had were the hands, or the hours.

In the office I held the pen in my fist like a child with a crayon and wrote the cause on the order, in my own hand, under the copperplate. It took three goes to make *pins* look like a word. Then I tore off the carbon slip, took two new steel hinge pins off a card in the box marked SPARES, and found the block plane.
Dusty got up when I did, the way he always does. On floor 5 he walked out of the lift ahead of me and turned into Walter, which is to say he stayed exactly the same dog and started talking.
"Door?"
"Door."

5-1 opens outwards, hinges on the corridor side. The door had dropped at the latch side and jammed into the frame at the top corner, and where it rubbed, the edge had drunk up the corridor's damp and swollen.
I knocked first. I waited. Nobody answered.
"It's the caretaker," I said to the door. "I'm going to do your hinges. I'm not coming in. I'll lift you a bit and take a shaving off your edge and you'll shut properly. You'll feel a knock."
Walter sat down on the lino. "You knocked."
"I knocked."
"That's the job," he said. "Pins are on your side. Go on."

I wedged the door and drove the bottom pin up with a nail punch held in my fist, which is not how anyone teaches you. The old pin came out worn to a waist, grey and shiny where the knuckles had ground on it for longer than I've been alive. The new one went in clean. It felt like what it was. Plain new steel, nothing in it.

Then the top pin. The door came up the width of a fingernail, and I eased the swollen edge with the plane where it still caught. The shavings came off damp. I kept my eyes on the hinges the whole time. It's nobody's business what's behind a door they weren't asked through.
The door closed with a click. I put the slip flat against it and signed it there.

``` WO-5-003.   FLOOR 5.   TIER 1. FAULT:                 DOOR 5-1 SWOLLEN IN FRAME. CAUSE:                 hinge pins worn thin with age. door dropped and bound. latch edge swelled where it rubbed. TAKEN BY:              R. Anand SIGNED OFF AT FAULT:   R. Anand ```
The heat went out of my hands like water out of a basin. The knuckles came back. I made a fist, a whole one, and opened it, and laughed out loud in an empty corridor.
"That's five," said Walter.
"Five what?"
"Five closed. Five's grade one, son. Odd-job."
"What does odd-job get me?"
"Your key'll open the common parts and the corridors. Up here and down. Not homes. Homes you still ask." He scratched his ear with a back foot. "And you can carry two now."
"I knew about the homes."
"You know it now," he said, and walked back to the lift.
In the office the header had changed while I was upstairs. The book doesn't need you to watch.
``` CARETAKER:   R. ANAND. GRADE:       1. ODD-JOB. CREDITS:     5. HOLDING:     NONE. CERTIFIED:   NONE. ```
Holding none. I looked at that for a long time. It was the first time since my second night that the book had nothing of mine in it.

It didn't last. At seven I took WO-5-006, the corridor lights, and carried a flicker at the edges of my eyes for the fifty minutes it took to find a cloth flex gone brittle in a ceiling rose and replace it. I signed it under the bulb, which stopped flickering, and so did I. Credits six. Then I made toast.
Then there was one order left on floor 5.

``` WO-5-005.   FLOOR 5.   TIER 1. FAULT:            SLAB. RISING DAMP. CAUSE:            UNDIAGNOSED. GRADE REQUIRED:   1. SYMPTOM:          COLD RISING FROM THE FEET. ACHE IN THE KNEES. STATUS:           TAKEN. ```
I signed for it at quarter past eight. The cold came into my socks first, like a puddle you didn't see, and then it climbed. By the time I reached the lobby my knees felt like a wet November.
The damp was in the slab under the void. The void was behind the panel. Behind the panel was the Felt.
I went up on my own. Dusty stayed on his mat. I didn't ask him.
I stood in front of the riser panel with my feet like two blocks of ice and knocked three times, the way you'd knock on a neighbour's door when you can hear the telly.
Nothing.

"It's the caretaker," I said. "Ravi. I've signed for your slab. The damp in it. It's in my knees now, I don't know how you've stood it. It's an old fault and nobody's doing, and I can't fix it from this side of the panel. So I'm asking. Can I come in?"
Nothing. Then, on the tea-coloured paint at eye height, a grey bloom came up through the gloss like breath on a cold window, and spread, and became letters.
YOU CAME IN BEFORE.
"I did," I said. "I'm sorry. I thought it was plant space, because it hadn't got a door, and I was wrong. It's your home, and I walked into it without knocking."
The letters faded back into the paint. New ones came, slowly. A mould does not hurry.
THE COMPLAINT STANDS.
"That's up to you. But the damp's mine now, whatever happens at midnight."
A long pause. My feet hurt.
THE DEEP IS WET. THE ROOTS DROWN.
"Then let me dry it." I put my hand flat on the panel, next to the letters, not on them. "Let me in, and you'll have a dry slab by midnight. I promise."
The letters went, and I had the feeling of being weighed by something with a lot of time.
DRY BY MIDNIGHT AND THE COMPLAINT COMES DOWN. WET AT MIDNIGHT AND IT STANDS.
"Done," I said.
COME IN. YOU KNOCKED.
I turned the four catches and opened the panel.
The void breathed out warm and wet, and the grey-white growth stirred under my torch. I kept the beam low. "If you wouldn't mind moving off where I'm working," I said, "I'll keep the light off you."

It moved. Not quickly. It drew back off the slab in the near corner like a cat getting off a chair it hadn't finished with, and left the concrete bare and dark and shining wet in a ring about a yard across. The key-eaters' old nest was in the far corner, green keys and white threads, and I didn't go near it.
The cold in my feet got worse the closer I got to the ring. That's how I found the middle.

Low on riser 2's offset, where an old brass tee joined the cast iron, a stub of lead pipe came off sideways and went down into a hole in the slab. A branch to somewhere that wasn't there any more, cut off long ago and its end closed. I couldn't see the end, but I could hear it. Every few seconds, from inside the hole, a drip.
The lead had been weeping into the slab for years. Not a leak you'd ever notice. Just enough, forever.
"There you are," I said to the pipe.
I couldn't write it there. The book's blank outside the office, and the cause goes in the book. So I closed the panel, said, "Back in a bit," to the paint, and went down.

At twenty to ten I wrote the cause on WO-5-005 in my own hand: *old lead branch off riser 2, sealed end split with age, weeping into slab*. Nobody did this. It was just old. I tore off the slip and found a new brass blanking plug the right thread for the tee.
I didn't take the blowlamp. You don't take a naked flame into somebody's house when the house is the somebody.
The tee would not let go of the lead.

I shut riser 2 off again, the way I had earlier, drained it down, and went at the old connector with two wrenches, one to hold and one to turn, and it held. Eighty years of scale. My knees had gone from aching to a deep wet throb, like the bones had gone soft, and I was kneeling on concrete that soaked the cold straight up into them.
"Come on," I said to the connector. "You've done your bit. You've held on to that branch since before anyone in this building was born. You can stop now. I'll put something better in. Come on."
It didn't move. I leant my whole weight on the wrench, and it still didn't move, and some time after eleven I sat back on my heels and talked to the Felt, which hadn't asked.
"I've got an hour," I said. "I said midnight. I meant midnight. I'm not stuck, I'm just slow."

Then I heard myself. Leaning harder on a seized nut is what you do when you've stopped thinking. So I put a block of wood against the nut and gave it three sharp taps with the hammer to crack the scale, the way you would on any site if you weren't kneeling in a mould's living room at eleven at night.

The nut turned, then it was spinning, and the stub of lead came away in my hand with a cough of black water. I held the plug in my palm there at the tee, feeling for the heaviness I'd felt in Jurek's tap earlier that day. There wasn't any. Grade one, which was all this needed. I taped its thread, my fingers doing what I told them again, and wound it into the tee, and nipped it up.
I turned riser 2 back on and watched the plug for ten minutes. Dry. I pulled the dead lead out of its hole, split at the bottom where somebody had folded it shut a long time ago.
The ring on the slab was still dark.
I knelt by the hole with the slip and the pen. My watch said 23:41.

``` WO-5-005.   FLOOR 5.   TIER 1. CAUSE:                 old lead branch off riser 2, sealed end split with age, weeping into slab. TAKEN BY:              R. Anand SIGNED OFF AT FAULT:   R. Anand ```

The cold went out of my feet all at once, like taking off wet boots. And the dark on the slab went back. It pulled in from the edges towards the hole the way a tide goes out across sand, quicker than any concrete has ever dried, and left the slab pale and dusty. Under my knees it was warm.
"Nineteen minutes," I said. "Told you."
The Felt came back across the bare concrete, slowly, and settled.
I shut the panel, turned all four catches, and walked up the corridor to the board.
The complaint was coming down. The grey letters went pale and powdery and dropped off the baize in a fine dust, word by word, until the board was green again. It was 23:44.
Then something grew across the empty baize in the same grey fur, one line, slowly.
OUR ROOTS GO FURTHER DOWN THAN YOUR BASEMENT, CARETAKER.
I read it twice. I took it for a parting shot, a mould having the last word, and said, "Good night," to the board, because I didn't have a better answer.
The lift doors opened to my key. I stepped in and reached for the B, and stopped.
Above the 5, where there had only ever been a painted-over hole, there was a brass button with a lamp behind a glass bead. It was lit.
The book was open on the desk when I got down. It always is.
``` CARETAKER:   R. ANAND. GRADE:       1. ODD-JOB. CREDITS:     7. HOLDING:     NONE. CERTIFIED:   5. ```
Floor 5's page was black from top to bottom. I turned it over.

Floor 6's page had filled in copperplate while I was upstairs. Nine orders, WO-6-001 to WO-6-009, all red. My eyes went past them, because underneath, after a gap where there were no numbers at all, there was one more.

``` WO-6-017.   FLOOR 6.   TIER 2. FAULT:            FLUE BACKDRAFT. CAUSE:            UNDIAGNOSED. GRADE REQUIRED:   2. SYMPTOM:          COUGH. DRY. ASSIGNED:         roll 4C STATUS:           ABANDONED. ```
The rest was copperplate. The assignment line wasn't. It was in square capitals, in ink gone brown with age, in a hand that wasn't mine and wasn't the book's.

Roll. I knew what that was. On a lead roof you dress the sheets over wooden rolls at the joints, and on a big job you number them. A flue backdraft could easily start at the flashing round a stack, if a roll had lifted and let the wind in. Roll 4C: which joint on which stack.
Then I read it again, the way I read everything, and my lips moved on the last two characters.
4C isn't a joint. 4C is a door at the top of the stairs with a brown coat and a pair of slippers behind it.
Roll, like a register. Like a list of names.
Mrs Wrobel's cough is dry. Jurek had a cough for years, she said.
I looked up at the walls of the office, at the old super's index cards pinned all round them, every one of them in square capitals. I didn't take one down to compare. I didn't need to.
I went up to the lobby. Dusty was asleep on his mat with his nose in his tail. I crouched down by him.
"I need you upstairs," I said. "Now, please."
He opened one eye. Then he got up, stiff in the back legs, followed me to the lift, and leant against my shins while I pressed the new button with a finger that bent.
The doors opened on floor 6 on dry, close heat, the smell of coke and old soot, and a dull orange glow far off in the dark. I didn't look at any of it.
Walter walked out onto the floor and turned round.
"Who wrote roll 4C in my book?" I said. "What's on Mrs Wrobel, Walter?"
He looked at me for a long time, a scruffy grey lurcher in the heat, with his ears down.
"Not yet, son," he said, and walked back into the lift.
